lesson.title: Judging Distance With Just One Eye
lesson.summary: Monocular depth cues let the visual system judge distance and depth using input from a single eye, or even a flat two-dimensional image, through cues like relative size, interposition, and linear perspective.
lesson.body:
Close one eye and the three-dimensional world does not suddenly flatten out entirely. Distant mountains still look far away, a road still appears to stretch off toward the horizon, and a nearby chair still looks closer than the wall behind it. This remains possible because the visual system has an entire second set of tools for judging depth that work with only one eye, known as monocular depth cues. Unlike binocular cues, which depend on comparing input from two eyes, monocular cues can be extracted from a single two-dimensional image, which is exactly why painters and photographers can create a convincing illusion of depth on a flat canvas or screen.

Several monocular cues rely on how objects relate to one another in a scene. Relative size uses the general expectation that among two objects assumed to be similar, the one that produces a smaller image on the retina is farther away. Interposition, also called overlap, relies on the fact that when one object partially blocks another from view, the blocking object is understood to be closer. Linear perspective uses the way parallel lines, such as the edges of a road or railroad tracks, appear to converge as they recede into the distance, with a sharper angle of convergence signaling greater distance.

Other monocular cues come from texture and lighting. Texture gradient describes how a uniformly textured surface, like a field of grass or a gravel driveway, appears to have finer, more densely packed detail as it recedes toward the horizon, and coarser, more distinct detail up close. Light and shadow provide cues because objects are generally understood to be illuminated from above, so the brain uses the pattern of highlights and shadows on a surface to infer its three-dimensional shape, which is why a photograph lit from an unusual angle can look strange or unsettling. Relative height also contributes, since objects positioned higher in the visual field, up to the horizon, are typically perceived as farther away.

One additional monocular cue, motion parallax, requires movement rather than a still image. When traveling in a car and looking out the side window, nearby objects like fence posts appear to zip by quickly while distant objects like mountains seem to move slowly or barely at all. The brain uses this difference in apparent speed to judge relative distance. Like binocular depth cues, all of these monocular cues depend on the visual system taking in raw, two-dimensional sensory information, the pattern of light striking the retina, and building it up piece by piece into a rich, organized sense of a three-dimensional world, which is why artists trained in techniques like linear perspective can trick a viewer's bottom-up processing into perceiving real depth on a surface that is, in physical fact, perfectly flat.
